content.author: stacy-jankowski
content.description: On a recording, your voice sounds foreign, almost embarrassing. The culprit is not the microphone: it is your skull, and the way your brain recognizes itself.

hero.hook: Videos of your friends do not bother you. But your own voice in a voice message makes you wince. Why does that one sound ring false?

blocks.text: What is the "self"? Philosophers, scientists and artists have been asking the question for centuries. To study it, researchers often use the image of the face, which everyone recognizes at a glance. But the voice matters just as much to the feeling of being oneself.

Hence the paradox. You can watch videos of your friends or family without any trouble. Then comes a voice message you recorded yourself, and you flinch: that voice is not mine. And yet it is. To understand why, you have to follow the path of the sound.

Speaking begins with a push of air. The diaphragm drives air out of the lungs and up into the throat. As it passes between the [[vocal cords]], it makes them vibrate at high speed: these vibrations, higher or lower in pitch, travel up the throat. The mouth and tongue then shape them into sounds and words.

Hearing is the reverse journey. Most sounds reach us through [[air conduction]]: the waves travel down the ear canal and make the eardrum vibrate, and the eardrum passes those vibrations to the tiny bones of the middle ear. Amplified, they reach the [[cochlea]], in the inner ear, where thousands of hair cells bristling with [[stereocilia]] bend and produce an electrical signal. The auditory nerve carries it to the brain, which identifies and sorts it.

blocks.caption: Mouse cochleas under the electron microscope, normal (left) and mutant: the rows of hair cells bristling with stereocilia.

blocks.text: When you listen to a recording of yourself, everything travels by air conduction, like any other sound. But when you speak, a second channel joins in: [[bone conduction]]. The mechanical vibrations of your voice spread directly through the bones of the skull to the inner ear, bypassing the eardrum and the middle ear.

blocks.caption: A tuning fork placed on the skull during a hearing test: the sound travels through bone, not air.

blocks.text: The cochlea therefore receives two signals at once, one from the air and one from the bones, and turns both into messages for the brain. In real time, your voice is a richer, more complex sound than anything a microphone can capture. The recording delivers only part of it.

That leaves the discomfort to explain. Researchers do not yet have a definitive answer, but one idea is appealing: the [[uncanny valley]] effect. The concept comes from robotics and animation. The more an artificial creature resembles a human, the more familiar and likeable it seems to us. Up to a point.

When the imitation gets very close without being perfect, sympathy turns into unease, even revulsion. A recording delivers only the airborne part of our voice, without the richness of bone conduction. We hear most of it, but not all. The brain lands in the uncanny valley: it is almost "me," but not quite.

The uncanny valley does not explain everything. A recording also shows only one facet of how we present ourselves to others. The voice is not fixed: we adjust it constantly to the context, often without thinking, and the sense of self is built on all those variations at once.

In a professional setting, most people lower their pitch to sound more composed. Faced with a baby or a pet, the voice climbs higher. Mouth, tongue and lips change their settings, and with them the version of "self" we let others hear.

The perception of self is therefore an elaborate construction, made of dozens of different voices. The brain has no single blueprint against which to match the recording. What it hears comes out of the microphone without passing through bone, frozen in a single register: close enough to be recognized, too different to be owned.

Your recorded voice sounds wrong because it lacks the bone conduction your skull adds when you speak, and because it freezes just one of your thousand versions: close enough to be recognized, not close enough to be accepted.

sections.title: One voice, a thousand versions of you

air conduction.explanation: The transmission of sound through the air: sound waves enter the ear canal, make the eardrum vibrate and then the small bones of the middle ear, before reaching the inner ear. It is the only channel through which you hear a recording of your own voice.

bone conduction.explanation: The transmission of sound through the bones of the skull, directly to the inner ear, bypassing the eardrum and the middle ear. When you speak, it adds to air conduction and enriches the voice you hear, something a recording cannot reproduce.

cochlea.explanation: A spiral-shaped organ in the inner ear, lined with hair cells. It turns vibrations, whether they arrive through the air or through the bones of the skull, into electrical signals that the auditory nerve carries to the brain. It is where the two paths of your own voice meet.

stereocilia.explanation: Tiny hair-like structures standing on the surface of the cochlea's hair cells. They bend in time with sound vibrations and trigger the electrical signal sent to the brain. Without them, no vibration would ever become a perceived sound.

uncanny valley.explanation: A notion from robotics and animation: an imitation of a human pleases us more the closer it gets, until, almost perfect but not quite, it provokes unease. A recorded voice, almost our own, may fall into it too.

vocal cords.explanation: Two folds of tissue in the larynx, at the top of the windpipe. Air driven out by the lungs makes them vibrate at high speed, which produces the sound of the voice, later shaped into words by the mouth and tongue.
